q: In the pumping lemma for CFLs, s = uvwxy must satisfy which conditions?
options: |vwx| ≤ p, |vx| ≥ 1, and uvⁱwxⁱy ∈ L for all i ≥ 0
|uv| ≤ p, |v| ≥ 1, and uvⁱwxy ∈ L for all i
explain: Two pieces, v and x, are pumped together. They sit inside a window of length at most p, and they are not both empty.
A stack can match one pair of counts, as in aⁿbⁿ and aⁿbⁿcᵐ, but not three equal counts. The pumping lemma proves aⁿbⁿcⁿ is not context-free.

q: Proving aⁿbⁿcⁿ is not context-free with s = aᵖbᵖcᵖ: what does |vwx| ≤ p guarantee?
options: vwx touches at most two of the three letter blocks
vwx lies entirely in the a's
v and x are both empty
explain: Each block has length p, so a window of at most p symbols cannot contain both an a and a c. At least one letter count is untouched by pumping.

q: In the pumping lemma for CFLs, one of v and x may be empty, as long as they are not both empty.
explain: True. The condition is |vx| ≥ 1. For example, v = ε and x non-empty is allowed, so proofs must handle that case too.

q: In the proof of the lemma, the repeated part comes from…
options: a variable that appears twice on a long path of a parse tree
a state that repeats in a DFA
a symbol that repeats on the stack
explain: In a tall CNF parse tree, some variable A repeats on a path. A ⇒* vAx can then be used any number of times, giving vⁱwxⁱ.
aⁿbⁿcᵐ needs only one matching pair, and wwᴿ is a mirror image, which a stack handles naturally. ww (a copy, not a mirror) and aⁿbⁿcⁿ are not context-free.

q: If a language satisfies the conditions of the CFL pumping lemma, it must be context-free.
explain: False. As with the regular lemma, it is only a necessary condition. It can show that a language is not context-free, but never that it is.

q: To prove {ww | w ∈ {a, b}*} is not context-free, a good choice is…
explain: Any window of length p can only touch neighbouring blocks, and pumping breaks the copy structure. (ab)ᵖ(ab)ᵖ and aᵖaᵖ can be pumped while staying in the language, and abab is too short.

q: Why does the CFL pumping lemma pump two substrings instead of one?
options: Recursion in a grammar, A ⇒* vAx, adds material on both sides of A at once
Because a PDA has two stacks
Because CFLs are closed under union
explain: A self-embedding variable wraps the inner part w: one copy of v goes on the left and one copy of x on the right, matched in number.

q: The pumping length p for a CFL comes from…
options: the size of a CNF grammar for L (its number of variables)
the number of states of a DFA
the length of the shortest word in L
the size of the alphabet only
explain: With m variables in CNF, any string longer than 2ᵐ has a parse-tree path long enough to repeat a variable. That gives p = 2ᵐ (or similar).
